summary: On the road south toward Jerusalem, four encounters. Pharisees test him about divorce and he answers by going back past Moses to creation. Disciples try to keep children away and he is indignant about it. A wealthy, decent man asks how to inherit eternal life, is told to sell everything, and walks away grieving — the only person in the gospels who declines a direct invitation. Jesus predicts his death a third time, James and John immediately ask for the best seats, and the chapter ends with a blind beggar who throws off his cloak and follows.
whyItMatters: Three times in this chapter someone approaches Jesus about status or reward, and every time he inverts it. Then a man with nothing — no name worth recording except his father's, no standing, shouting from a roadside — asks for the one thing anybody in this book has actually needed: to see.

context.author: Anonymous; early tradition names Mark, recording Peter's preaching
context.audience: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea; verse 12 addresses a woman divorcing her husband, which was possible under Roman law but not Jewish — a sign of who Mark is writing for
context.setting: Judea and beyond the Jordan, then Jericho — the last stop before the eighteen-mile climb up to Jerusalem
context.literaryForm: Travel narrative. The whole section from 8:27 to 10:52 is framed as a walk, and it is bracketed by two blind men receiving sight

outline.heading: Divorce
outline.note: A test question answered from Genesis rather than from the divorce law

outline.heading: Little children
outline.note: The disciples turn them away; he is indignant and takes them in his arms

outline.heading: The man with great possessions
outline.note: Mark alone records that Jesus looked at him and loved him

outline.heading: Camels and needles
outline.note: The disciples are astonished; Peter points out what they have given up

outline.heading: Third prediction
outline.note: The most detailed of the three — mocking, spitting, flogging, death

outline.heading: James and John ask for thrones
outline.note: The other ten are furious, and he uses the moment to define leadership

outline.heading: Bartimaeus
outline.note: Told to be quiet, shouts louder, throws off his cloak, and follows on the road

keyVerses.text: Jesus looking at him loved him, and said to him, “One thing you lack. Go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me, taking up the cross.”
keyVerses.why: The hard instruction comes with affection attached. Mark is the only gospel that records the look.

keyVerses.text: With men it is impossible, but not with God, for all things are possible with God.
keyVerses.why: The answer to 'then who can be saved?' — which is asked, notice, about rich people.

keyVerses.text: For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
keyVerses.why: The closest thing in Mark to a statement of why he is going to die, and it is spoken to settle an argument about promotion.

keyVerses.text: What do you want me to do for you?
keyVerses.why: The identical question he asked James and John ten verses earlier. Compare the two answers.

questions.question: Why is the divorce question a 'test'?
questions.answer: Two reasons. There was a live rabbinic dispute over how broadly the grounds in Deuteronomy 24:1 should be read — one school allowed divorce for almost any cause, another only for serious misconduct — so any answer would offend somebody. And the geography matters: Mark places this beyond the Jordan, in Herod Antipas's territory. The last person who spoke publicly about the marriage of a ruler out here was beheaded in chapter 6.

questions.question: Is Jesus saying Moses got it wrong?
questions.answer: He says Moses wrote that commandment because of hardness of heart — a concession to a situation, not a description of the design. Then he goes further back, to Genesis, for what marriage was for. Worth knowing what the certificate of divorce actually did in that world: it protected a divorced woman by documenting she was free to remarry, without which she was destitute and vulnerable. Jesus is not attacking the protection; he is refusing to let a protection be treated as a permission.

questions.question: Does this passage mean divorce is always forbidden?
questions.answer: Christians have not agreed, and the differences are long-standing rather than careless. Matthew's version of this saying includes an exception for sexual unfaithfulness (Matthew 19:9), and Paul addresses another case in 1 Corinthians 7:15. Catholic teaching holds a valid sacramental marriage indissoluble, with annulment addressing whether a real marriage existed. Orthodox practice permits remarriage after divorce in some circumstances as a pastoral concession. Most Protestant traditions recognize the Matthew and Paul exceptions. What is common ground: Jesus raises the bar on how seriously marriage is taken, and does it in a setting where women bore most of the cost of easy divorce.

questions.question: Why does verse 12 mention a woman divorcing her husband?
questions.answer: Because Jewish law of the period did not give women that option — a wife could petition, but the act was the husband's. Under Roman law she could initiate it. So this half of the saying only makes practical sense for readers living under Roman rather than Jewish law, and it is one more small piece of evidence about where Mark's audience was.

questions.question: What does 'receive the kingdom like a little child' mean? Childlike faith?
questions.answer: Probably less about innocence or trust than about position. Children in that world received everything and could earn nothing; they had no claim, no standing, and nothing to negotiate with. Sandwiched as this is between a question about grounds for divorce and a man asking what he must do to inherit eternal life, the point lands as: you come into this with empty hands, not with a case. Note also that Jesus is indignant — a strong word — at the disciples for gatekeeping.

questions.question: Why does Jesus push back on being called 'good'?
questions.answer: The reply — why do you call me good, no one is good except God — has been read two ways. Some take it as a denial of his own divinity; others as the opposite, a question designed to make the man think about what he has just said, since Jesus never elsewhere confesses a fault. What is clear in context is that the man arrives with a transactional frame: good teacher, what must I do, I have kept all these. Jesus's first move is to unsettle the categories he brought with him.

questions.question: Does everyone have to sell everything?
questions.answer: The instruction is given to one man, and Mark shows Jesus accepting hospitality from people who kept their houses. But the passage does not let wealthy readers off lightly either — the general statements that follow are sweeping, and the disciples' shock in verse 26 shows they heard them as such. The most careful reading: the command names what actually held this particular man, and Jesus asked for it because he loved him. The question the passage puts to any reader is what occupies the same position for them.

questions.question: Was there a gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye that camels had to kneel to enter?
questions.answer: No. That explanation is medieval and there is no evidence for such a gate. It softens the saying into a lesson about humility and effort, which is the opposite of the point. Jesus means an actual camel and an actual sewing needle — the largest animal in the region and the smallest opening — and the disciples' reaction confirms they heard it as impossible. That is why his answer in verse 27 is about impossibility, not technique.

questions.question: Verse 30 promises a hundred times more — houses, family, land. Is that a prosperity promise?
questions.answer: Read the whole verse. The list of returns has two things attached that are easy to skip: 'with persecutions,' and 'in the age to come, eternal life.' The list also drops one item that was in the original — fathers are given up but not returned, which fits a community that calls God Father. What is being described looks less like compensation and more like what happens when people who have left households find themselves inside a much larger one, trouble included.

questions.question: James and John ask for thrones right after he describes being tortured and killed. How?
questions.answer: It is the third time this pattern runs — prediction, then a display of total incomprehension (8:32, 9:34, 10:35) — and Mark builds it deliberately. They have heard 'and after three days rise again' and skipped to what comes after the victory. His reply asks whether they can drink his cup and share his baptism, both images of what is coming, and tells them they will. Tradition holds James was the first apostle executed and John suffered exile. They got what they asked for, in a form they had not imagined.

questions.question: What does 'ransom for many' mean?
questions.answer: The Greek word was used for the price paid to free a slave or a prisoner of war. Applied here it says his death buys someone's release, which is why this verse sits behind a great deal of later Christian thinking about the cross. Two things the verse does not settle, and readers have argued about both: who the payment is made to, and whether 'many' means a limited group or is a Semitic way of saying 'a great number' as opposed to a few. Note where it is placed — not in a sermon, but at the end of an argument about who gets the best seat.

questions.question: Why does Mark name Bartimaeus when so many others go unnamed?
questions.answer: It stands out — most people healed in this gospel are anonymous. The usual explanation is that he was known in the community that preserved the story, possibly still alive when it was told. Notice also what he does: he calls Jesus 'son of David,' a messianic title, and nobody silences him. He throws off his cloak, which for a beggar was both bedding and the thing he collected coins on. And the last line says he followed him on the road — the road that goes to Jerusalem.

glossary.def: A written document releasing a wife to remarry. In practice it functioned as a protection for the woman, which is worth holding alongside Jesus's argument about why it was permitted.
From Genesis 2:24. A statement about a new single unit formed from two people, which is the basis of the argument in verses 6-9.
In this period, life in the age to come — the world set right after God's decisive intervention. Not primarily a description of duration.
The price paid to release a slave or captive. Verse 45 applies the word to Jesus's death.
Both used in verse 38 as images of what Jesus is about to undergo. 'Cup' in the Hebrew scriptures often means an allotted portion of suffering, and he uses it again in Gethsemane (14:36).
A messianic title, claiming descent from Israel's greatest king. Bartimaeus shouts it in public and is not corrected — the first time in Mark that happens.
